claims.text: A transfer-learned machine-learning model can predict electronic conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr across 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The proposed model will be more accurate than traditional analytical models based on perfect, defect-free crystals.
Relevant bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimens contain typical microstructural imperfections.
Some HfNbTaTiZr specimens contain approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The model will be pre-trained on high-entropy-alloy data containing defect and oxygen-impurity effects and fine-tuned on HfNbTaTiZr data.
Conductivity measurements are available in the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The high-temperature measurements include HfNbTaTiZr specimens containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Lattice defects and dispersed oxygen impurities modify electron scattering and electronic transport.
Oxygen has a perturbative effect on defect physics in related alloys that can be transferred to HfNbTaTiZr.
Perfect-crystal analytical predictions omit additional scattering and electronic-state modifications caused by defects and oxygen.
Accounting for defect-induced scattering and electronic-state modifications will allow the model to reproduce measured conductivity trends more accurately.
At 300 K, the proposed model is expected to predict conductivity near 1.5×10^5 S/m.
The model will capture low-temperature conductivity variations caused by defect-induced scattering.
Perfect-crystal analytical models have significant discrepancies relative to experimental conductivity measurements.
The predictive advantage applies to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing up to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen and within 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Accuracy may be limited for virtually oxygen-free specimens, specimens with substantially more than 1 wt.% oxygen, or temperatures outside the stated ranges.
Transfer learning has produced analogous predictive improvements in similar high-entropy alloys.
